- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Mummification played a crucial role in ancient Egyptian culture, preserving the body for the afterlife.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The Egyptians believed the soul (ka) needed a physical body to inhabit in the afterlife.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The heart was left in the mummy, while the brain and other organs were removed and stored in canopic jars.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The mummification process took around 70 days and involved several stages: removal of internal organs, dehydration with natron, embalming, wrapping, and placing protective amulets.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Mummification was a status symbol, only affordable for the wealthy and high-ranking officials.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Mummification ensured the individual's ka could return to the body, allowing them to enjoy the afterlife.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The Egyptians believed mummification granted immortality and was integral to funerary practices.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Anubis was the god dedicated to protecting the dead and guiding them through the afterlife.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The oldest known mummy, "Gebelein Man," dates back to around 3500 BCE.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The art of mummification was lost after the Roman conquest of Egypt in 30 BCE.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Sarcophagi served as protective barriers for mummies and symbolized the womb, representing the mother goddess Isis.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Sarcophagi were often decorated with images of gods and goddesses associated with rebirth, such as Osiris and Isis.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The oldest known sarcophagus dates back to around 2600 BCE.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The Great Pyramid of Giza is essentially a massive sarcophagus.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The American Museum of Natural History has exhibits on ancient civilizations, including the Hall of Human Origins.
